author.name: Apollonius of Rhodes
author.lead: Apollonius of Rhodes was an ancient Greek author, best known for the Argonautica, an epic poem about Jason and the Argonauts and their quest for the Golden Fleece. The poem is one of the few extant examples of the epic genre and it was both innovative and influential, providing Ptolemaic Egypt with a "cultural mnemonic" or national "archive of images", and offering the Latin poets Virgil and Gaius Valerius Flaccus a model for their own epics. His other poems, which survive only in small fragments, concerned the beginnings or foundations of cities, such as Alexandria and Cnidus, which were places of interest to the Ptolemies, whom he served as a scholar and librarian at the Library of Alexandria.

Argonautica.title: Argonautica
Argonautica.lead: The Argonautica is a Greek epic poem written by Apollonius Rhodius in the 3rd century BC. The only entirely surviving Hellenistic epic (though Callimachus's Aetia is substantially extant through fragments), the Argonautica tells the myth of the voyage of Jason and the Argonauts to retrieve the Golden Fleece from remote Colchis. Their heroic adventures and Jason's relationship with the Colchian princess/sorceress Medea were already well known to Hellenistic audiences, which enabled Apollonius to go beyond a simple narrative, giving it a scholarly emphasis suitable to the times. His epic incorporates his research in geography, ethnography, comparative religion, and Homeric literature. However, his main contribution to the epic tradition lies in his development of the love between hero and heroine – he seems to have been the first narrative poet to study "the pathology of love".

summaries.heading: Book 1
summaries.text: The poem begins with an invocation to Apollo and briefly recounts his prophetic warning to Pelias, king of Iolcus, that his downfall will be the work of a man with only one sandal. Jason has recently emerged as the man in question, having lost a sandal while crossing a swollen stream. Consequently, Pelias has entrusted him with a suicidal mission to Colchis to bring back the Golden Fleece. A ship, the Argo, has already been constructed by Argus, a shipwright working under Athena's instructions. Meanwhile, a band of heroes has arrived to help in the venture. The locals marvel at such a gathering – young Jason has been given an impossible mission yet this band of heroes just might help him pull it off. His mother fears the worst. He bids her to stay strong and calm. Jason urges the heroes to elect a leader for the voyage. They all nominate Heracles.

summaries.heading: Book 2
summaries.text: The Argonauts reach a gulf in the Propontis, home to the Bebrycians, whose king Amycus demands a boxing match with the champion of these "sea-wanderers" (Ancient Greek: ἁλίπλαγκτοι). He does this with all travellers and he doesn't even ask who they are. Angered by such disrespect, Polydeukes volunteers and the fight begins. Amycus is a man-mountain but the young Argonaut is skilled with his fists and eventually lands a lethal blow. The Bebrycians rush on the victor, weapons drawn, but they are intercepted and chased off by his rampant crewmates. Some sheep are herded on board and the Argo leaves the following day. Their next stop is on the opposite coast, near the home of Phineus, once a king of the Thynians. He too doesn't ask who these travellers are. He already knows.

summaries.heading: Book 3
summaries.text: The third book begins by invoking Erato, the Muse of love poetry. The Argo is still hidden in a Colchis backwater when the goddesses Hera and Athena retire to a private room on Olympus to consider in secret how best to help Jason. Hera thinks the daughter of the Colchian king might prove useful if she could be made to fall in love with him. She then suggests enlisting the help of Aphrodite. Athena likes the plan but, being a virgin conscious of appearances, asks Hera to do all the talking. They find the goddess of love indolently combing her hair in her apartment. She has been bickering with her young son Eros and doubts if the unruly child will fire any arrows at Medea just to please her.

summaries.heading: Book 4
summaries.text: The poet calls upon the Muse to describe Medea's state of mind: is it shame, alarm, or love that leads her to flee Colchis? Her treason is already known to her father and self-poisoning seems like an option again. She decides instead to flee Colchis with her nephews, the sons of Phrixus, camped with the Argonauts by the river. Doors open for her by magic as she hurries barefoot though the palace, and the moon laughs at her outdoors, recalling the many times that she was captured and brought to earth by Medea's cruel love spells (a reference to the moon's passion for Endymion). Arriving at the camp, Medea warns the others about her father's treachery and offers to help steal the Golden Fleece from its guardian serpent.

history.heading: Background
history.text: The Argonautica was an adventure for the poet, one of the major scholars of the Alexandrian period – it was a bold experiment in re-writing Homeric epic in a way that would meet the demanding tastes of his contemporaries. According to some accounts, a hostile reception even led to Apollonius's exile to Rhodes. The literary fashion was for small, meticulous poems, featuring displays of erudition and paradoxography (the account of marvels and oddities), as represented by the work of Callimachus. In adapting the epic genre to this audience, Apollonius went a long way towards inventing the romance novel, including narrative techniques like the "interior monologue", whereby the author identifies with a character's thoughts and feelings.

history.heading: Some issues
history.text: A "Callimachian epic"? Callimachus set the standards for Hellenistic aesthetics in poetry and, according to ancient sources, he engaged in a bitter literary feud with Apollonius. Modern scholars generally dismiss these sources as unreliable and point to similarities in the poetry of the two men. Callimachus, for example, composed a book of verses dealing with aitia, the mythical origins of contemporary phenomena. According to one survey, there are eighty aitia in Argonautica. Yet Argonautica is clearly intended to be fundamentally Homeric and therefore seems at odds with the fashionable poetics of Callimachus. The epic hero? Addressing the issue of heroism in Argonautica, the German classicist H. Fränkel once noted some unheroic characteristics of Jason and his crew.

history.heading: Date of the poem
history.text: There is some dispute about the date when the poem was originally published. It could have been during the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus (283–246 BC), or a generation later. According to the astronomical analysis of the poem by Jackie Murray, the poem commemorates the year 238 BC, implying that it was published at the time of Ptolemy III Euergetes (246–221 BC) as the majority of ancient sources claim.

secondary.heading: Sources
secondary.text: Apollonius's Argonautica was based on multiple ancient sources, including Homer and Pindar. The story of the expedition seems to have been known to the author of the Odyssey (xii. 69, &c.), who states, that the ship Argo was the only one that ever passed between the whirling rocks (petrai planktai Πλαγκταὶ; Planctae, after the encounter with the Clashing Rocks). Jason is mentioned several times in the Iliad (vii. 467, &c., xxi. 40, xxiii. 743, &c.), but not as the leader of the Argonauts. Hesiod (Theog. 992, &c.) relates the story of Jason saying that he fetched Medea at the command of his uncle Pelias, and that she bore him a son, Medeius, who was educated by Cheiron.

Q102884.label: Mnemosyne
Q102884.description: personification of memory in Greek mythology, mother of the nine muses
Q102884.lead: In Greek mythology, Mnemosyne was one of the Titans, who are the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). She was the goddess of memory and the mother of the nine Muses by Zeus.

Q103107.label: Leto
Q103107.description: Greek mythological figure and mother of Apollo and Artemis
Q103107.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Leto is the mother of Apollo and Artemis. She is the daughter of the Titans Coeus and Phoebe, and the sister of Asteria.

Q103975.label: Calliope
Q103975.lead: In Greek mythology, Calliope is the Muse who presides over eloquence and epic poetry, so called from the ecstatic harmony of her voice. Hesiod and Ovid called her the "Chief of all Muses".

Q104042.label: Terpsichore
Q104042.description: muse of dance in Greek mythology
Q104042.lead: In Greek mythology, Terpsichore is one of the nine Muses and goddess of dance and chorus. She lends her name to the word "terpsichorean", which means "of or relating to dance".

Q104413.label: Erato
Q104413.lead: In Greek mythology, Erato is one of the Muses, associated with erotic lyric poetry. The name would mean "desired" or "lovely", if derived from the same root as Eros, as Apollonius of Rhodes playfully suggested in the invocation to Erato that begins Book III of his Argonautica.

Q1045732.label: Mimas
Q1045732.lead: In Greek mythology, Mimas was one of the Gigantes (Giants), the offspring of Gaia, born from the blood of the castrated Uranus.

Q1075014.label: Argus
Q1075014.description: mythological Greek character, builder of Argo
Q1075014.lead: In Greek mythology, Argus was the builder and eponym of the ship Argo, and consequently one of the Argonauts; he was said to have constructed the ship under Athena's guidance. Argus was commissioned to build the Argo by King Pelias (ruler of Iolcus) so that the crew that would come to be known as the Argonauts could find and bring the Golden Fleece back to Iolcus, which was in Thessaly.

Q108419.label: Rhea
Q108419.description: female Titan in Greek mythology, mother of Zeus and mother of Hera
Q108419.lead: In Greek mythology, Rhea, Rhia or Rheia was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). She was the sister and wife of Cronus, and by him was the mother of Hestia, Demeter, Hera, Hades, Poseidon, and Zeus.

Q109220.label: Boreas
Q109220.description: Greek mythological personification and god of the North wind, storms,, winter, loneliness, solitude, absence, lack, sadness, depression, calmness and serenity
Q109220.lead: Boreas is the Greek god of the cold north wind, storms, and winter. Although he was normally taken as the north wind, the Roman writers Aulus Gellius and Pliny the Elder both took Boreas as a northeast wind, equivalent to the Roman god Aquilo or Septentrio.

Q1119537.label: Phaethusa
Q1119537.description: daughter of Helios and Neaera, in Greek mythology
Q1119537.lead: In Greek mythology, Phaethusa or Phaëthusa was a daughter of the sun god Helios. She and her sister Lampetia watched over their father's sacred herds of cattle and sheep on the island of Thrinacia (Sicily or Malta).

Q1124866.label: Lynceus
Q1124866.description: mythical brother of Ida, son of Aphareus
Q1124866.lead: Lynceus is in Greek mythology a Messenian prince and one of the Argonauts who served as a lookout on the Argo. He also participated in the hunt for the Calydonian boar.

Q11294144.label: Castor
Q11294144.description: Greek mythical figure, brother of Pollux

Q1129489.label: Orithyia
Q1129489.lead: In Greek mythology, Orithyia or Oreithyia was an Athenian princess who was raped by Boreas, the north wind, and gave birth to the twin Boreads, Zetes and Calaïs.

Q1129914.label: Libya
Q1129914.description: goddess in Roman and Greek mythology
Q1129914.lead: Libya, Libye, Lybie or Lybee was the daughter of Epaphus, King of Egypt, in both Greek and Roman mythology. She personified the land of Ancient Libya in North Africa, and was considered by the Greeks to be the origin of the name of what is now Libya.

Q1136130.label: Idas
Q1136130.description: son of Aphareus, husband of Marpessa, argonaut in Greek mythology
Q1136130.lead: In Greek mythology, Idas, was a Messenian prince. He was one of the Argonauts, a participant in the hunt for the Calydonian Boar, and contender with the gods.

Q1170101.label: Melas
Q1170101.description: son of Phrixus, figure of Greek mythology

Q1171925.label: Dascylus
Q1171925.description: son of Lycus in Greek mythology

Q11921121.label: Aethra
Q11921121.lead: In Greek mythology, Aethra or Aithra was a Troezenian princess and the daughter of King Pittheus.

Q12046224.label: Pollux
Q12046224.description: Greek mythical figure, brother of Castor

Q121973.label: Eros
Q121973.description: Greek god of love and sex
Q121973.lead: Eros is the Greek god of love and sex. The Romans referred to him as Cupid or Amor.

Q122248.label: Heracles
Q122248.description: divine hero in Greek mythology, son of Zeus and Alcmene
Q122248.lead: Heracles, born Alcaeus (Ἀλκαῖος) or Alcides (Ἀλκείδης) was the greatest of the Greek heroes. He was considered the son of Zeus and Alcmene, and the foster son of Amphitryon.

Q1230535.label: Thoas
Q1230535.description: father of Hypsipyle in ancient Greek mythology, son of Dionysus
Q1230535.lead: In Greek mythology, Thoas was a son of the god Dionysus and Ariadne, the daughter of the Cretan king Minos. He was the king of Lemnos when the Lemnian women decided to kill all the men on the island.

Q12878261.label: Itymoneus
Q12878261.description: character from Greek mythology, son of Hypeirochus

Q1301614.label: Macris
Q1301614.description: daughter of Aristaeus in Greek mythology
Q1301614.lead: In Greek mythology, Macris, also called Nysa (Ancient Greek: Νύσα), is a daughter of Aristaeus who reared the goddess Hera in her youth, before incurring the wrath of the goddess and being banished by her.

Q1301972.label: Butes
Q1301972.description: Argonaut, son of Teleon in Greek Mythology

Q130818.label: Atlas
Q130818.lead: In Greek mythology, Atlas is a Titan condemned to hold up the heavens or sky for eternity after the Titanomachy. Atlas also plays a role in the myths of two of the greatest Greek heroes: Heracles (Hercules in Roman mythology) and Perseus.

Q130832.label: Perseus
Q130832.description: legendary Greek hero and founder of Mycenae, demigod son of Zeus and Danae; famous for beheading the Gorgon Medusa
Q130832.lead: In Greek mythology, Perseus is the legendary founder of the Perseid dynasty. He was, alongside Cadmus and Bellerophon, the greatest Greek hero and slayer of monsters before the days of Heracles.

Q131090.label: Chaos
Q131090.lead: In the context of religious cosmogony, Chaos refers to the division of reality outside or in contrast to the ordered cosmos. As such it refers to a state, place, or time beyond the known, familiar, and reliable world, often said to be inhabited by strange, ominous, or demonic beings.

Q131575.label: Hecate
Q131575.lead: Hecate is a goddess in ancient Greek religion and mythology. Variously associated with crossroads, night, light, magic, witchcraft, and the Moon, she is most often shown holding a pair of torches, a key, or snakes, or accompanied by dogs, and in later periods she is typically depicted as three-formed or triple-bodied.

Q131585.label: Selene
Q131585.description: ancient Greek goddess and personification of the Moon, daughter of Hyperion and Theia
Q131585.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Selene is the goddess and personification of the Moon. Also known as Mene (Ancient Greek: μήνη pronounced [mɛ̌ː.nɛː] MEH-neh), she is traditionally the daughter of the Titans Hyperion and Theia, and sister of the sun god Helios and the dawn goddess Eos.

Q131588.label: Ganymede
Q131588.description: son of Tros in Greek mythology
Q131588.lead: In Greek mythology, Ganymede ( GAN-im-eed) or Ganymedes is a divine hero whose homeland was Troy. Homer describes Ganymede as the most handsome of mortals and tells the story of how he was abducted by the gods to serve as Zeus's cup-bearer in Olympus.

Q1320718.label: Theseus
Q1320718.description: legendary king of Athens, son of Aegeus and Aethra; famous for slaying the Minotaur
Q1320718.lead: Theseus was a divine hero in Greek mythology, famous for slaying the Minotaur. The myths surrounding Theseus, his journeys, exploits, and friends, have provided material for storytelling throughout the ages.

Q1333108.label: Perse
Q1333108.description: Oceanid (one of the three thousand daughters of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys), and the wife of the Sun god, Helios
Q1333108.lead: In Greek mythology, Perse or Perseis (Περσηίς, Persēís) is one of the 3,000 Oceanids, fresh water-nymph daughters of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys. Perse married Helios, the god of the Sun, and bore him several children, most notably Circe, the sorceress-goddess of Aeaea.

Q134270.label: Helios
Q134270.description: Greek god and personification of the Sun
Q134270.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Helios is the god who personifies the Sun. His name is also Latinized as Helius, and he is often given the epithets Hyperion ("the one above") and Phaethon ("the shining").

Q143880.label: Athamas
Q143880.description: son of Minyas or Aeolus in Greek mythology
Q143880.lead: In Greek mythology, Athamas was a Boeotian king.

Q1466343.label: Minyas
Q1466343.lead: In Greek mythology, Minyas was the founder of Orchomenus, Boeotia.

Q148030.label: Triton
Q148030.description: Greek god, messenger of the sea
Q148030.lead: Triton is a Greek god of the sea, the son of Poseidon and Amphitrite. Triton lived with his parents in a golden palace on the bottom of the sea.

Q150986.label: siren
Q150986.description: creatures half bird and half woman who lured sailors by the sweetness of her song
Q150986.lead: In Greek mythology, sirens are female humanlike beings with alluring voices; they appear in a scene in the Odyssey in which Odysseus saves his crew's lives. Roman poets place them on some small islands called Sirenum Scopuli.

Q1539539.label: Sinope
Q1539539.lead: In Greek mythology, Sinope was a daughter of Asopus (a river god) and the eponym of the city Sinope on the Black Sea's south coast. Sinope is connected romantically to two gods, Apollo and Zeus.

Q1539620.label: Oeagrus
Q1539620.lead: In Greek mythology, Oeagrus was a king of Thrace, and father of Orpheus.

Q159168.label: Themis
Q159168.description: in ancient Greek mythology, a titaness, the personification of divine order, fairness, law, natural law, and custom, whose symbols are the scales of justice
Q159168.lead: In Greek mythology and religion, Themis is the goddess and personification of justice, divine order, law, and custom. She is one of the twelve Titan children of Gaia and Uranus, and the second wife of Zeus.

Q161419.label: Oceanus
Q161419.description: ancient Greek god of the earth-encircling river, Oceanos
Q161419.lead: In Greek mythology, Oceanus or Okeanos was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth), and the god of the great river which encircled the entire world. He was the brother and husband of the Titaness Tethys, and by her was the father of the river gods and the Oceanids.

Q16331922.label: Erginus
Q16331922.lead: In Greek mythology, Erginus was an Argonaut who piloted the Argo after the helmsman Tiphys died.

Q1638536.label: Lampetia
Q1638536.description: daughter of Helius in Greek myth
Q1638536.lead: In Greek mythology, Lampetia also spelled Lampetie, was a daughter of the sun god Helios. She and her sister Phaethusa watched over their father's prized herds of cattle and sheep on the island of Thrinacia (Sicily).

Q16515491.label: Amphidamas
Q16515491.description: Greek mythical character, Argonaut, son of Aleus

Q165170.label: Europa
Q165170.description: Phoenician character in Greek mythology, daughter of Agenor
Q165170.lead: In Greek mythology, Europa was a Phoenician princess said to have been abducted by Zeus in the form of a bull. She was the mother of the Cretan king Minos.

Q165938.label: Hesperides
Q165938.lead: In Greek mythology, the Hesperides are the nymphs who tend the garden in which grow the trees of Hera which bear golden apples. They were also called the Atlantides (Ancient Greek: Ἀτλαντίδες, romanized: Atlantídes) from their reputed father, Atlas.

Q16933131.label: Melite
Q16933131.lead: In Greek mythology, Melite was one of the Naiads, daughter of the river god Aegaeus, and one of the many loves of Zeus and his son Heracles. Given the choice, she chose Heracles over Zeus who went off in search of other pursuits.

Q172549.label: Aeolus
Q172549.description: god of winds, son of Hippotes in Greek mythology
Q172549.lead: In Greek mythology, Aeolus, the son of Hippotes, was the ruler of the winds encountered by Odysseus in Homer's Odyssey. Aeolus was the king of the island of Aeolia, where he lived with his wife and six sons and six daughters.

Q174278.label: Medea
Q174278.description: daughter of King Aeëtes of Colchis in Greek mythology
Q174278.lead: In ancient Greek mythology, Medea is the daughter of King Aeëtes of Colchis. Medea is known in most stories as a sorceress, an accomplished pharmakís, a worker in pharmakeía (medicinal magic), and is often depicted as a high priestess of the goddess Hecate.

Q174353.label: Orpheus
Q174353.description: legendary musician, poet, and prophet in ancient Greek religion and myth
Q174353.lead: In Greek mythology, Orpheus was a Thracian bard, legendary musician and prophet. He was also a renowned poet and, according to legend, travelled with Jason and the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece, and descended into the underworld to recover his lost wife, Eurydice.

Q176758.label: Jason
Q176758.description: Greek mythological hero, son of Aeson
Q176758.lead: Jason was an ancient Greek mythological hero and leader of the Argonauts, whose quest for the Golden Fleece is featured in Greek literature. He was the son of Aeson, the rightful king of Iolcos.

Q178417.label: Eos
Q178417.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Eos is the goddess and personification of the dawn, who rose each morning from her home at the edge of the river Oceanus to deliver light and disperse the night. She opened the gates of heaven for her brother Helios (the Sun), to pass through, and was imagined in poetry and art as a radiant, often winged goddess driving her horse-drawn chariot across the sky, bringing with her the colours and dew of morning.

Q178641.label: Peleus
Q178641.description: son of Aeacus in Greek mythology
Q178641.lead: In Greek mythology, Peleus was a hero, king of Phthia, husband of Thetis and the father of their son Achilles.

Q179014.label: Io
Q179014.description: nymph seduced by Zeus in Greek mythology
Q179014.lead: In Greek mythology, Io was one of the mortal lovers of Zeus. An Argive princess, her descendants included Perseus, Cadmus, Heracles, Minos, Lynceus, Cepheus, Dionysus, and Danaus.

Q179209.label: Hyperion
Q179209.lead: In Greek mythology, Hyperion was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). With his sister, the Titaness Theia, Hyperion fathered Helios (Sun), Selene (Moon) and Eos (Dawn).

Q1795211.label: Cyzicus
Q1795211.description: Greek mythical character, King of the Doliones
Q1795211.lead: In Greek mythology, King Cyzicus or Kyzikos was the ruler of the Dolionians, a tribe that inhabited the southern shore of the Propontis (the Sea of Marmara). He gave his name to a city of the same name, Cyzicus, his capital.

Q179543.label: Iapetos
Q179543.lead: In Greek mythology, Iapetus or Iapetos, also Japetus or Japetos, was one of the Titans, the son of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth) and father of Atlas, Prometheus, Epimetheus, and Menoetius. He was also called the father of Buphagus and Anchiale in other sources.

Q180222.label: Amphitrite
Q180222.description: Oceanid or Nereid of Greek mythology
Q180222.lead: In ancient Greek mythology, Amphitrite was the goddess of the sea, the queen of the sea, and her consort is Poseidon. She was a daughter of Nereus and Doris (or Oceanus and Tethys).

Q181360.label: harpies
Q181360.description: half-human and half-bird personification of storm winds from Greek and Roman mythology generally depicted as birds with the heads of maidens
Q181360.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, a harpy is a half-human and half-bird mythical creature, often believed to be a personification of storm winds. They feature in Homeric poems.

Q182019.label: Leda
Q182019.description: daughter of Thestius in Greek mythology
Q182019.lead: In Greek mythology, Leda, also rendered as Lede, was an Aetolian princess who became queen consort of Sparta through her marriage to King Tyndareus. Zeus fell in love with Leda, and to avoid his wife Hera's jealousy, assaulted her while disguised as a swan.

Q182439.label: Pelias
Q182439.description: mythical king of Iolcus, and son of Poseidon who sent Jason on the quest for the Golden Fleece
Q182439.lead: Pelias was king of Iolcus in Greek mythology. He was the one who sent Jason on the quest for the Golden Fleece.

Q182837.label: Coeus
Q182837.description: Titan in Greek mythology, one of the twelve titans
Q182837.lead: In Greek mythology, Coeus, also called Koios or Polus, was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth).

Q183281.label: Phoebe
Q183281.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Phoebe was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). She is a goddess of intellect and prophecy.

Q183417.label: Chiron
Q183417.lead: In Greek mythology, Chiron, also Cheiron or Kheiron, was held to be the superlative centaur amongst his brethren since he was called the "wisest and justest of all the centaurs".

Q184216.label: Tethys
Q184216.description: ancient Greek mythological figure; mother of the river gods and the Oceanids
Q184216.lead: In Greek mythology, Tethys was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth), the sister and wife of the Titan Oceanus, and the mother of the river gods and the Oceanids. Although Tethys had no active role in Greek mythology and no established cults, she was depicted in mosaics decorating baths, pools, and triclinia in the Greek East, particularly in Antioch and its suburbs, either alone or with Oceanus.

Q184232.label: Theia
Q184232.description: female Titan in Greek mythology; mother of Helios, Selene and Eos
Q184232.lead: In Greek mythology, Theia also called Thea, Thia, Euryphaessa, Aethra or Basileia, was one of the Titans, the children of Uranus (Sky) and Gaia (Earth). Her brother-husband is Hyperion, a god of the light, and together they are the parents of Helios (the Sun), Selene (the Moon), and Eos (the Dawn).

Q184437.label: Thetis
Q184437.lead: Thetis is a figure from Greek mythology with varying mythological roles. She mainly appears as a sea nymph, a goddess of water, and one of the 50 Nereids, daughters of the ancient sea god Nereus.

Q184570.label: Iris
Q184570.description: the personification of the rainbow in ancient Greek religion and mythology
Q184570.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Iris is a daughter of the gods Thaumas and Electra, and the personification of the rainbow. She functions as a messenger and servant to the Olympians, particularly Hera.

Q184874.label: Ariadne
Q184874.description: the daughter of Minos in Greek mythology
Q184874.lead: In Greek mythology, Ariadne was a Cretan princess as the daughter of King Minos. There are multiple variations of Ariadne's myth, but she is best known for helping Theseus escape from the Minotaur and being abandoned by him on the island of Naxos.

Q1862400.label: Phrontis
Q1862400.description: son of Phrixus in Greek mythology
Q1862400.lead: In Greek mythology, Phrontis or Phrontides was one of four (or five) sons of Phrixus and Chalciope (Iophossa), daughter of King Aeetes of Colchis. His brothers were Cytissorus, Argus and Melas, and according to some accounts, also of Presbon.

Q187602.label: Circe
Q187602.lead: In Greek mythology, Circe is a witch and goddess. In most accounts, Circe is described as a daughter of the sun god Helios and the Oceanid Perse.

Q189527.label: Nereus
Q189527.lead: In Greek mythology, Nereus was the eldest son of Pontus (the Sea) and Gaia (the Earth). Nereus and Doris became the parents of 50 daughters (the Nereids) and a son (Nerites), with whom Nereus lived in the Aegean Sea.

Q190323.label: Atalanta
Q190323.description: Greek mythological character, the only female Argonaut
Q190323.lead: Atalanta is a heroine in Greek mythology. There are two versions of the huntress Atalanta: one from Arcadia, whose parents were Iasus and Clymene and who is primarily known from the tales of the Calydonian boar hunt and the Argonauts; and the other from Boeotia, who is the daughter of King Schoeneus and is primarily noted for her skill in the footrace.

Q190543.label: Alkmene
Q190543.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcmene or Alcmena ( alk-MEE-nə; Doric Greek: Ἀλκμάνα, romanized: Alkmána; Latin: Alcumena; meaning "strong in wrath") was the wife of Amphitryon, by whom she bore two children, Iphicles and Laonome. She is best known as the mother of Heracles, whose father was the god Zeus.

Q190563.label: Pontus
Q190563.lead: In Greek mythology, Pontus is the personification of the sea. In Hesiod's Theogony (8th or 7th century BC), he is the offspring of Gaia (the Earth), who produces him alone.

Q190565.label: Metis
Q190565.description: Oceanid of Greek mythology, goddess of wisdom, daughter of Oceanid and Tethys
Q190565.lead: Metis, in ancient Greek religion and mythology, was the pre-Olympian goddess of wisdom, counsel and deep thought, and a member of the Oceanids. She is notable for being the advisor and first wife of Zeus, the king of the gods.

Q191725.label: Aegeus
Q191725.lead: Aegeus was one of the kings of Athens in Greek mythology, who gave his name to the Aegean Sea, was the father of Theseus, and founded Athenian institutions.

Q192082.label: Charybdis
Q192082.description: figure in Greek mythology transformed in a sea monster by Zeus
Q192082.lead: Charybdis is a sea monster in Greek mythology. Along with the sea monster Scylla, she appears as a challenge to epic characters such as Odysseus, Jason, and Aeneas.

Q192946.label: Tyndareus
Q192946.lead: In Greek mythology, Tyndareus was a Spartan king.

Q19828218.label: Oenoe
Q19828218.description: nymph in mythology, wife of Thoas

Q203480.label: Phaethon
Q203480.description: son of Helios from Greek mythology
Q203480.lead: Phaethon, also spelled Phaëthon, is the son of the Oceanid Clymene and the sun god Helios in Greek mythology. According to most authors, Phaethon is the son of Helios who, out of a desire to have his parentage confirmed, travels to the sun god's palace in the east.

Q205233.label: Maia
Q205233.lead: In ancient Greek mythology, Maia, also spelled Maie, is one of the Pleiades and the mother of the messenger god Hermes by Zeus. Maia was identified with the Roman earth goddess Maia, the mother of Mercury.

Q206187.label: Aeacus
Q206187.description: son of Zeus in Greek mythology
Q206187.lead: Aeacus was a king of the island of Aegina in Greek mythology. He was a son of Zeus and the nymph Aegina, and the father of the heroes Peleus and Telamon.

Q212087.label: Eurystheus
Q212087.description: king of Mycenae in Greek mythology
Q212087.lead: In Greek mythology, Eurystheus was king of Tiryns, one of three Mycenaean strongholds in the Argolid, although other authors including Homer and Euripides cast him as ruler of Argos.

Q2293816.label: Endeïs
Q2293816.description: daughter of Sciron in Greek mythology
Q2293816.lead: In Greek mythology, Queen Endeïs was the wife of King Aeacus and mother of the heroes Telamon and Peleus (since Peleus was the father of Achilles and Telamon was the father of Ajax the Great and Teucer, Endeïs was the grandmother of Achilles, Ajax and Teucer). The name is a dialect variant of Engaios (Ἐγγαῖος, "in the earth").

Q2293877.label: Eidyia
Q2293877.description: Oceanid of Greek mythology, spouse of Aeetes
Q2293877.lead: In Greek mythology, Idyia or Eidyia (Ancient Greek: Εἰδυῖα, romanized: Eidyîa; ) was a daughter of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys, and queen to Aeëtes, king of Colchis. She was the mother of Medea, Chalciope and Absyrtus.

Q2310293.label: Amphithemis
Q2310293.description: Greek mythical character, son of Apollo and Acacallis

Q23168.label: Minos
Q23168.description: Greek mythology character, son of Zeus and Europa, king of Crete
Q23168.lead: In Greek mythology, Minos was a king of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa. Every nine years, he made King Aegeus pick seven young boys and seven young girls to be sent to Daedalus's creation, the labyrinth, to be eaten by the Minotaur.

Q2394140.label: Nasamon
Q2394140.description: Greek mythical character, son of Amphithemis und Tritonis

Q241971.label: Aeëtes
Q241971.description: son of Helios in Greek mythology
Q241971.lead: Aeëtes, or Aeeta, was the ruler of the eponymous realm of Aea in Greek mythology, a wondrous realm which from the fifth century B.C.E. onward became identified with the kingdom of Colchis east in the Black Sea. The name comes from the ancient Greek word αἰετός (aietós, "eagle").

Q250588.label: Astraeus
Q250588.description: Greek astrological god associated with winds
Q250588.lead: In Greek mythology, Astraeus or Astraios is the son of Crius and Eurybia and the consort of Eos (goddess of the dawn). He is said to be the father of the winds.

Q2623901.label: Caphaurus
Q2623901.description: son of Garamas in Greek mythology

Q2627407.label: Polyphemus
Q2627407.lead: In Greek mythology, Polyphemus was a Greek hero and also an Argonaut from Larissa.

Q2718542.label: Alcimede
Q2718542.description: Greek mythological character, mother of Jason
Q2718542.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcimede was one of the matrilineal Minyan daughters, the daughter of Clymene, Minyas' daughter.

Q272000.label: Deianira
Q272000.description: wife of Heracles in Greek mythology
Q272000.lead: Deianira, Deïanira, or Deianeira, also known as Dejanira, is a Calydonian princess in Greek mythology whose name translates as "man-destroyer" or "destroyer of her husband". She was the wife of Heracles and, in late Classical accounts, his unwitting murderer, killing him with the poisoned Shirt of Nessus.

Q272047.label: Endymion
Q272047.description: son of Aethlius in Greek mythology
Q272047.lead: In Greek mythology, Endymion was variously a handsome Aeolian shepherd, hunter, or king who was said to rule and live at Olympia in Elis. He was also venerated and said to reside on Mount Latmus in Caria, on the west coast of Asia Minor.

Q274600.label: Ladon
Q274600.lead: Ladon was a dragon in Greek mythology, who guarded the golden apples in the Garden of the Hesperides.

Q27613.label: Cadmus
Q27613.description: mythological founder of Thebes, son of Agenor
Q27613.lead: In Greek mythology, Cadmus was the legendary founder of Boeotian Thebes. He was, alongside Perseus and Bellerophon, the greatest hero and slayer of monsters before the days of Heracles.

Q28708056.label: Paraebius
Q28708056.description: friend or slave of Phineus in Greek mythology
Q28708056.lead: In Greek mythology, Paraebius is a Thracian man, a subject of king Phineus of Salmydessus. For years Paraebius suffered greatly due to an injustice committed by his father against a hamadryad nymph, until advice from Phineus led him to salvation.

Q317932.label: Argo
Q317932.description: ship of Jason and the Argonauts in Greek mythology
Q317932.lead: In Greek mythology, the Argo was the ship of Jason and the Argonauts. The ship was built with divine aid and carried the Argonauts on their quest for the Golden Fleece from Iolcos to Colchis.

Q321298.label: Aegina
Q321298.description: nymph, eponym of the island Aegina
Q321298.lead: Aegina was a figure of Greek mythology, the nymph of the island that bears her name, Aegina, lying in the Saronic Gulf between Attica and the Peloponnesos. The archaic Temple of Aphaea, the "Invisible Goddess", on the island was later subsumed by the cult of Athena.

Q321541.label: Meleager
Q321541.description: son of Oeneus in Greek mythology, king of Calydon
Q321541.lead: Meleager was a hero in Greek mythology, venerated in his temenos at Calydon in Aetolia. He was famed as the host of the Calydonian boar hunt in the epic tradition that was reworked by Homer, and was also mentioned as one of the Argonauts.

Q3268516.label: Lycus
Q3268516.description: Greek mythical character, son of Dascylus

Q331327.label: Telamon
Q331327.description: one of the Argonauts of Jason, in Greek mythology
Q331327.lead: Telamon in Greek mythology was the son of King Aeacus of Aegina, and Endeïs, a mountain nymph. The elder brother of Peleus, Telamon sailed alongside Jason as one of his Argonauts, and was present at the hunt for the Calydonian Boar.

Q332752.label: Hylas
Q332752.description: mythical character, companion of Heracles abducted by nymphs
Q332752.lead: In classical mythology, Hylas was a youth who served Heracles (Roman Hercules) as companion and servant. His abduction by water nymphs was a theme of ancient art, and has been an enduring subject for Western art in the classical tradition.

Q333658.label: Absyrtus
Q333658.lead: In Greek mythology, Absyrtus or Apsyrtus Ancient Greek: Άψυρτος) was a Colchian prince and brother or half-brother of Medea. He was involved in Jason's escape with the golden fleece from Colchis.

Q336428.label: Hellen
Q336428.lead: In Greek mythology, Hellen is the eponymous progenitor of the Hellenes. He is the son of Deucalion (or Zeus) and Pyrrha, and the father of three sons, Dorus, Xuthus, and Aeolus.

Q34201.label: Zeus
Q34201.description: Greek god of the sky and king of the gods
Q34201.lead: Zeus is the supreme deity of the Greek pantheon. He is a sky and thunder god in ancient Greek religion and mythology, who rules as king of the gods on Mount Olympus.

Q3499376.label: Sthenelus
Q3499376.description: son of Actor in Greek mythology

Q35500.label: Aphrodite
Q35500.description: Greek goddess of love, beauty, pleasure, and procreation
Q35500.lead: Aphrodite is an ancient Greek goddess associated with love and beauty. Aphrodite's main cult centers were Cythera, Cyprus, Corinth, and Athens.

Q3622209.label: Arete
Q3622209.description: person in Greek mythology, wife of Alcinous
Q3622209.lead: In Greek mythology, Queen Arete of Scheria was the wife of Alcinous and mother of Nausicaa and Laodamas.

Q3678283.label: Cytissorus
Q3678283.description: Founder of Cytorus in Greek mythology
Q3678283.lead: In Greek mythology, Cytisorus or Cytorus (Κυτώρου) or Cylindrus was the founder of Cytorus.

Q3680839.label: Cleite
Q3680839.lead: In Greek mythology, the name Clite or Cleite may refer to: Clite, daughter of Danaus and Memphis, married and killed Cleitus, son of Aegyptus and Tyria. Clite, a maenad who followed Dionysus on his Indian campaign.

Q3704804.label: Deileon
Q3704804.lead: Deileon may refer to two figures in Greek mythology. Deileon, a Triccan prince as son of King Deimachus in Thessaly.

Q371206.label: Astypalaea
Q371206.description: lover of Poseidon in Greek mythology
Q371206.lead: In Greek mythology, Astypalaea or Astypalaia or Astypale was a Phoenician princess as the daughter of King Phoenix and Perimede, daughter of Oeneus; thus she was the sister of Europa. In some accounts, her mother was called Telephe and her siblings were Peirus and again Europe.

Q37122.label: Athena
Q37122.description: goddess of wisdom and war in ancient Greek religion and mythology
Q37122.lead: Athena or Athene, often given the epithet Pallas, is an ancient Greek goddess associated with wisdom, warfare, and handicraft who was later syncretised with the Roman goddess Minerva and Etruscan Menrva. Athena was regarded as the patron and protectress of various cities across Greece, particularly the city of Athens, from which she most likely received her name.

Q37340.label: Apollo
Q37340.description: god in Greek and later Roman mythology
Q37340.lead: Apollo is one of the Olympian deities in ancient Greek religion and mythology. His numerous functions include light, healing, prophecy, music, poetry, and archery.

Q38012.label: Hera
Q38012.description: Greek goddess, wife and sister of Zeus
Q38012.lead: In ancient Greek religion, Hera is the goddess of marriage, women, and family, and the protector of women during childbirth. In Greek mythology, she is queen among the twelve Olympians on Mount Olympus, sister and wife of Zeus, and daughter of the Titans Cronus and Rhea.

Q385397.label: Glaucus
Q385397.lead: In Greek mythology, Glaucus was a Greek prophetic sea-god, born mortal and turned immortal upon eating a magical herb. It was believed that he came to the rescue of sailors and fishermen in storms, having earlier earned a living from the sea himself.

Q391010.label: Chalciope
Q391010.lead: Chalciope, in Greek mythology, was a Colchian princess as the daughter of King Aeëtes. Acusilaus, Hesiod and Hesychius referred to her as Iophossa (Ιoφώσσης) while according to Pherecydes, she was called Euenia (Εύηνίαν).

Q391379.label: Achelous
Q391379.lead: Achelous (also Acheloos or Acheloios) was the god in ancient Greek religion and mythology associated with the Achelous River, the largest river in Greece. According to Hesiod, he was the son of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys.

Q392435.label: Aristaeus
Q392435.lead: Aristaeus was the mythological culture hero credited with the discovery of many rural useful arts and handicrafts, including beekeeping. He was the son of the huntress Cyrene and Apollo.

Q392631.label: Agenor
Q392631.description: mythical Phoenician king, father of Cadmus
Q392631.lead: Agenor was in Greek mythology and history a Phoenician king of Tyre or Sidon. The Greek historian Herodotus (c.

Q393261.label: Cyrene
Q393261.description: nymph, mother of Aristaeus by Apollo
Q393261.lead: In Greek mythology, Cyrene, also spelled Kyrene, was the etymon of the Greek colony of Cyrene, Libya. She was said to have been a Thessalian princess and huntress who became the queen regnant of Cyrene, founded and named in her honor by the god Apollo.

Q39503.label: Artemis
Q39503.description: goddess of the hunt and the wild in ancient Greek religion and mythology
Q39503.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Artemis is the goddess of hunting, the wilderness, wild animals, transitions, nature, vegetation, childbirth, care of children, and chastity. She was often said to roam the forests and mountains, attended by an entourage of nymphs.

Q398524.label: Philyra
Q398524.lead: In Greek mythology, Philyra or Phillyra was one of the 3,000 Oceanids, water-nymph daughters of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys.

Q4024302.label: Zetes
Q4024302.description: son of Boreas in Greek mythology

Q40901.label: Ares
Q40901.description: Greek god of war and combat
Q40901.lead: Ares is the Greek god of war and courage. He is one of the Twelve Olympians, and the son of Zeus and Hera.

Q410082.label: Aeson
Q410082.description: father of Jason in Greek mythology
Q410082.lead: In Greek mythology, Aeson was a king of Iolcus in Thessaly. He was the father of the hero Jason.

Q410417.label: Aethalides
Q410417.lead: In Greek mythology, Aethalides was one of the Argonauts together with his paternal step-brothers Erytus and Echion. He was a son of Hermes and Eupolemeia, a daughter of King Myrmidon of Phthia.

Q41127.label: Poseidon
Q41127.description: one of the twelve Olympians presiding over the sea, storms, earthquakes and horses
Q41127.lead: Poseidon is one of the twelve Olympians in ancient Greek religion and mythology, presiding over the sea, storms, earthquakes and horses. He was the protector of seafarers and the guardian of many Hellenic cities and colonies.

Q41484.label: Hermes
Q41484.description: Olympian god in Greek religion and mythology; the emissary and messenger of the gods; the god of trade, heraldry, merchants, commerce, roads, thieves, trickery, sports, travelers, and athletes; the son of Zeus and the Pleiad Maia
Q41484.lead: Hermes is an Olympian deity in ancient Greek religion and mythology considered the herald of the gods. He is also widely considered the protector of human heralds, travelers, thieves, merchants, and orators.

Q416384.label: Acastus
Q416384.lead: Acastus is a character in Greek mythology. He sailed with Jason and the Argonauts, and participated in the hunt for the Calydonian Boar.

Q41680.label: Dionysus
Q41680.description: ancient Greek god of winemaking and wine
Q41680.lead: In ancient Greek religion and myth, Dionysus is the god of wine-making, orchards, fruit, vegetation, fertility, festivity, insanity, ritual madness, religious ecstasy, and theatre. He was also known as Bacchus (Ancient Greek: Βάκχος Bacchos) by the Greeks (a name later adopted by the Romans) for a frenzy he is said to induce called baccheia.

Q41746.label: Achilles
Q41746.description: Greek mythological hero of the Trojan War
Q41746.lead: In Greek mythology, Achilles or Achilleus (Ancient Greek: Ἀχιλλεύς, romanized: Achilleús) was a hero of the Trojan War who was known as being the greatest of all the Greek warriors. The central character in Homer's Iliad, he was the son of the Nereid Thetis and Peleus, king of Phthia and famous Argonaut.

Q44204.label: Cronus
Q44204.description: ruler of the Titans in Greek mythology
Q44204.lead: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Cronus, Cronos, or Kronos was the leader and youngest of the Titans, the children of Gaia (Earth) and Uranus (Sky). Cronus castrated and overthrew his father and then ruled during the mythological Golden Age until he himself was overthrown by his son, Zeus, and imprisoned in Tartarus.

Q44384.label: Hephaestus
Q44384.lead: Hephaestus is the Greek god of artisans, blacksmiths, carpenters, craftsmen, fire, metallurgy, metalworking, sculpture, and volcanoes. In Greek mythology, Hephaestus was the son of Hera, either on her own or by her husband Zeus.

Q45967.label: Persephone
Q45967.description: Greek goddess of the seasons and the queen of the underworld; married with Hades
Q45967.lead: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Persephone is the daughter of Zeus and Demeter. She became the queen of the underworld after her abduction by her uncle Hades, the king of the underworld, who later took her into marriage.

Q48961.label: Calypso
Q48961.lead: In Greek mythology, Calypso was a nymph who lived on the island of Ogygia, where, according to Homer's Odyssey, she detained Odysseus for seven years against his will. She promised Odysseus immortality if he would stay with her, but Odysseus preferred to return home.

Q492938.label: Mopsus
Q492938.description: seer in Greek mythology, son of Ampyx
Q492938.lead: In Greek mythology, Mopsus, was the Lapith son of Ampyx and a nymph (sometimes named as Chloris and sometimes named Aregonis), born at Titaressa in Thessaly, was also a seer and augur. In Thessaly the place name Mopsion recalled his own.

Q496595.label: Alcinous
Q496595.description: mythical character, King of the Phaeacians, son of Nausithous and brother of Rhexenor
Q496595.lead: In Greek mythology, Alcinous was a son of Nausithous and brother of Rhexenor. After the latter's death, he married his brother's daughter Arete who bore him Nausicaa, Halius, Clytoneus and Laodamas.

Q54230.label: Nereids
Q54230.description: sea nymphs in Greek mythology, daughters of Nereus
Q54230.lead: In Greek mythology, the Nereids or Nereides are sea nymphs (female spirits of sea waters), the 50 daughters of the 'Old Man of the Sea' Nereus and the Oceanid Doris, sisters to their brother Nerites.

Q542356.label: Cleopatra
Q542356.description: Greek mythological figure, daughter of Boreas
Q542356.lead: In Greek mythology, Cleopatra was the name of the following women: Cleopatra, one of the fifty Danaids, the daughters of Danaus. Cleopatra, daughter of King Tros of Troy and Callirhoe, daughter of the river-god Scamander.

Q59697.label: Hesperus
Q59697.description: personification of the planet Venus or its manifestation in the evening
Q59697.lead: In Greek mythology, Hesperus is the Evening Star, the planet Venus in the evening. A son of the dawn goddess Eos (Roman Aurora), he is the half-brother of her other son, Phosphorus (also called Eosphorus; the "Morning Star").

Q6019476.label: Furies
Q6019476.description: vengeful deities of the Roman mythology

Q603759.label: Theras
Q603759.lead: Theras was a regent of Sparta, a son of Autesion and the brother of Aristodemos' wife Argeia, a Cadmid of Theban descent. He served as regent for his nephews Eurysthenes and Procles.

Q622781.label: Asopus
Q622781.lead: Asopus or Asopos is the name of four different rivers in Greece and one in Turkey. In Greek mythology, it was also the name of the gods of those rivers.

Q622809.label: Pyrrha
Q622809.description: daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora in Greek mythology
Q622809.lead: In Greek mythology, Pyrrha is the daughter of Epimetheus and Pandora, or of Prometheus.

Q624551.label: Nephele
Q624551.description: cloud goddess, wife of Athamas and mother of Phrixus and Helle
Q624551.lead: In Greek and Roman mythology, Nephele called Nebula by Latin authors, is the name of two figures associated with clouds, who figure respectively in the stories of Ixion and in the story of Phrixus and his sister Helle.

Q641065.label: Phineus
Q641065.description: son of Agenor in Greek mythology
Q641065.lead: In Greek mythology, Phineus was a king of Salmydessus in Thrace and seer, who appears in accounts of the Argonauts' voyage. Some accounts make him a king in Paphlagonia or in Arcadia.

Q644692.label: Corcyra
Q644692.description: daughter of the Asopos river and the nymph Metope
Q644692.lead: In Greek mythology and religion, Corcyra or Korkyra is the naiad daughter of the river-god Asopos and the nymph Metope, herself the daughter of the river-god Ladon. She is the personification and tutelary goddess of the ancient Greek city and island of Korkyra, now better known as Corfu.

Q654257.label: Tiphys
Q654257.lead: In Greek mythology, Tiphys was the helmsman of the Argonauts.

Q657174.label: Talos
Q657174.lead: In Greek mythology, Talos, also spelled Talus or Talon (Greek: Τάλων, Tálōn), was a man of bronze who protected Crete from pirates and invaders. Despite the popular idea that he was a giant, no ancient source states this explicitly.

Q668054.label: Talaus
Q668054.description: son of Bias in Greek mythology
Q668054.lead: In Greek mythology, Talaus was the king of Argos and one of the Argonauts. He was the son of Bias (or Perialces) and Pero, and brother of Arëius and Leodocus.

Q675699.label: Epaphus
Q675699.description: mythical character, son of Zeus and Io
Q675699.lead: In Greek mythology, Epaphus, also called Apis or Munantius was a son of Zeus and king of Egypt.

Q697942.label: Amycus
Q697942.description: in Greek mythology, the king of the Bebryces, a mythical people in Bithynia
Q697942.lead: In Greek mythology, Amykos, Latinized as Amycus, was the king of the Bebryces, a mythical people in Bithynia.

Q726279.label: Doris
Q726279.lead: Doris, in Greek mythology, was a sea goddess. She was one of the 3,000 Oceanids, daughters of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys.

Q743482.label: Phrixus
Q743482.description: son of Athamas in Greek mythology
Q743482.lead: In Greek mythology Phrixus was the son of Athamas, king of Boeotia, and Nephele (a goddess of clouds). He was the older brother of Helle and the father of Argus, Phrontis, Melas and Cytisorus by Chalciope (Iophassa), daughter of Aeetes, king of Colchis.

Q748144.label: Idmon
Q748144.description: son of Abas in Greek mythology
Q748144.lead: In Greek mythology, Idmon was an Argonaut seer.

Q748574.label: Asterodeia
Q748574.description: nymph, mother of Apsyrtus with Aeetes

Q749123.label: Euphemus
Q749123.description: son of Poseidon in Greek mythology
Q749123.lead: In Greek mythology, Euphemus was counted among the Calydonian hunters and the Argonauts, and was connected with the legend of the foundation of Cyrene.

Q749966.label: Oeneus
Q749966.lead: In Greek mythology, Oeneus was a Calydonian king. He was the first who received a vine-plant from Dionysos.

Q775296.label: Hypsipyle
Q775296.description: queen of Lemnos, granddaughter of Ariadne and Dionysos in Greek mythology
Q775296.lead: In Greek mythology, Hypsipyle was a queen of Lemnos, and the daughter of King Thoas of Lemnos, and the granddaughter of Dionysus and Ariadne. When the women of Lemnos killed all the males on the island, Hypsipyle saved her father Thoas.

Q776139.label: Semele
Q776139.description: mother of Dionysus in Greek mythology
Q776139.lead: In Greek mythology, Semele, or Thyone (Ancient Greek: Θυώνη, romanized: Thyṓnē), was the youngest daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, and the mother of Dionysus by Zeus (her own great-grandfather). Certain elements of the cult of Dionysus and Semele came from the Phrygians.

Q79999.label: Uranus
Q79999.description: primordial Greek deity, god of the Sky; one of the Greek primordial deities
Q79999.lead: In Greek mythology, Uranus, sometimes written Ouranos (Ancient Greek: Οὐρανός, lit. 'sky', [uːranós]), is the personification of the sky and one of the Greek primordial deities. According to Hesiod, Uranus was the son and husband of Gaia (Earth), with whom he fathered the first generation of Titans.

Q80493.label: Nausithous
Q80493.description: son of Poseidon in Greek mythology
Q80493.lead: The name Nausithous is shared by the following characters in Greek mythology: Nausithous, the king of the Phaeacians who reigned in the generation before Odysseus washed ashore on their home island of Scherie (his son Alcinous was king at the time of Odysseus's arrival). He was the son of the god Poseidon and Periboea, the daughter of the Giant king Eurymedon.

Q83160.label: Prometheus
Q83160.description: Titan, culture hero, and trickster figure in Greek mythology who defied the gods; son of Iapetus
Q83160.lead: In Greek mythology, Prometheus is a Titan who is responsible for creating and aiding humanity in its earliest days. He defied the Olympian gods by stealing fire from them and giving it to humanity.

Q833826.label: Nauplius
Q833826.description: king of Nauplia, son of Poseidon in Greek mythology

Q836525.label: Heliades
Q836525.description: daughters of Helios in Greek mythology
Q836525.lead: In Greek mythology, the Heliades were the daughters of Helios and Clymene, an Oceanid nymph. They were also called Phaethontides (Ancient Greek: Φαεθοντίδες, lit. 'daughters of Phaethon'), due to "Phaethon" being a common epithet for Helios.

Q836792.label: Klymene
Q836792.lead: In Greek mythology, Clymene or Klymene is the name of one of the three thousand Oceanid nymphs, usually the wife of Iapetus and mother by him of Prometheus, Epimetheus, Atlas and Menoetius.

Q869665.label: Cretheus
Q869665.description: in Greek mythology, king and founder of Iolcus

Q9286479.label: Harmonia
Q9286479.lead: In Greek mythology, Harmonia was a nymph, perhaps a naiad or dryad, in the glens of the Akmonian wood. She was the lover of Ares of whom she bore the warrior-women race of the Amazons.

Q93172.label: Gaia
Q93172.description: Greek primordial deity, the personification of the Earth
Q93172.lead: In Greek mythology, Gaia, also spelled Gaea, is the personification of Earth. She is the mother of Uranus (Sky), with whom she conceived the Titans (themselves parents of many of the Olympian gods), the Cyclopes, and the Giants, as well as of Pontus (Sea), from whose union she bore the primordial sea gods.

Q947753.label: Acacallis
Q947753.description: daughter of Minos in Greek mythology
Q947753.lead: Acacallis in Greek mythology, was princess of Crete. The Bibliotheca calls her Acalle (Ἀκάλλη).

Q975447.label: Oileus
Q975447.description: mythical father of Ajax the Lesser
Q975447.lead: In Greek mythology, Oileus or Oïleus was the king of Locris, and an Argonaut.
